import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 688
*Reference:*
- [erdosproblems.com/688](https://www.erdosproblems.com/688)
- [Er80] Erdős, Paul, _A survey of problems in combinatorial number theory_. Ann. Discrete Math. (1980), 89-115.
-/

open Real Filter

namespace Erdos688

/--
Define $\epsilon_n$ to be maximal such that there exists some choice of congruence class $a_p$
for all primes $n^{\epsilon_n} < p \leq n$ such that every integer in $[1,n]$ satisfies at least
one of the congruences $\equiv a_p \pmod p$.
-/
def Erdos688Prop (n : ℕ) (ε : ℝ) : Prop :=
  ∃ (a : ℕ → ℕ), ∀ (m : ℕ), 1 ≤ m → m ≤ n →
    ∃ (p : ℕ), p.Prime ∧ (n : ℝ)^ε < p ∧ p ≤ n ∧
      a p ≡ m [MOD p]

noncomputable def epsilonFunction (n : ℕ) : ℝ := sSup {ε : ℝ | Erdos688Prop n ε}

/--
Estimate $\epsilon_n$ - lower bound.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_688.parts.i.lower_bound :
    (answer(sorry) : ℕ → ℝ) =O[atTop] epsilonFunction := by
  sorry

/--
Estimate $\epsilon_n$ - upper bound.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_688.parts.i.upper_bound :
    epsilonFunction =O[atTop] (answer(sorry) : ℕ → ℝ) := by
  sorry

/--
In particular, is it true that $\epsilon_n = o(1)$?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_688.parts.ii : answer(sorry) ↔
    epsilonFunction =o[atTop] (fun (n : ℕ) ↦ (1 : ℝ)) := by
  sorry

/--
Erdős claims in [Er80] (p. 106) that it is not difficult to prove
$\epsilon_n \gg \frac{\log\log\log n}{\log\log n}$.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_688.variants.lglglg_over_lglg_is_big_o :
    (fun (n : ℕ) ↦ (log (log (log (n : ℝ)))) / (log (log (n : ℝ))))
      =O[atTop] epsilonFunction := by
  sorry

end Erdos688

reformulations.difference: The source calls ε_n “maximal” despite using the strict cutoff n^ε < p. The Lean definition uses the supremum, which need not itself be admissible.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: For n > 1 admitting a covering, let q be the largest prime threshold for which primes q ≤ p ≤ n can cover [1,n]. This maximum exists because only finitely many primes are available. The exponents admissible with the strict cutoff are exactly ε < log(q)/log(n): a covering using primes at least q works for every such ε; conversely, the least prime used by any strict-cutoff covering is a feasible threshold exceeding n^ε and cannot exceed q. Thus the supremum is precisely the intended extremal threshold log(q)/log(n), which is attained with a weak cutoff. The known positive lower bound ensures nonempty admissible sets for sufficiently large n, so exceptional small-input totalizations do not affect any stated asymptotic claim. Lean experiments prove equality of the strict- and weak-cutoff suprema for every n ≥ 2, and ε(3) = log(2)/log(3) with nonattainment. The full finite-threshold characterization was checked mathematically, not proved in Lean.
